items.prompt: Where in the nose does smell actually get detected?

options.label: Across the whole lining of the nostrils
options.feedback: Most of the inside of the nose just warms and moistens air; only a small patch is doing the detecting.

options.label: In a small patch high up inside the nasal cavity
options.feedback: The cells that detect odours are gathered into a patch set into the roof of the nasal cavity.

options.label: Inside the nostril hairs themselves
options.feedback: Those hairs filter out large particles like dust; smell detection happens further inside, on separate cells.

options.label: At the very tip, closest to the outside air
options.feedback: The tip of the nose is mostly cartilage and skin — the detecting cells sit further inside, up near the roof.

items.ok_line: The detecting cells sit off the main path that ordinary breathing takes.
items.ko_title: Not the whole lining, not the hairs, not the tip
items.ko_line: Smell is detected by one small patch, not spread across the whole nose.
items.exp_title: A small patch tucked up high
items.exp_text: The cells that actually detect odours are gathered into a small patch of tissue set into the roof of the nasal cavity, above the main path that quietly breathed air normally takes. Ordinary calm breathing sends just a trickle of air up to that patch, letting the rest pass by underneath without being smelled in any detail.

items.prompt: Why do odour molecules have to pass through a layer of mucus before they can be detected?

options.label: Mucus filters out molecules that are too small
options.feedback: Size isn't the issue mucus deals with here; it's about getting a molecule to dissolve and reach the receptor.

options.label: Mucus warms the air before it's smelled
options.feedback: Warming happens earlier, in the main airway; the thin layer over the receptors isn't there to adjust temperature.

options.label: Mucus blocks bacteria from reaching the smell receptors
options.feedback: Catching bacteria is something mucus does elsewhere in the airway, but it isn't why odour detection needs a wet surface.

options.label: The receptor cells only respond to molecules once they're dissolved
options.feedback: A molecule has to dissolve into the mucus film before it can fit into a receptor and trigger a signal.

items.ok_line: A dry molecule drifting past isn't enough on its own — it has to cross into the liquid first.
items.ko_title: Not filtering, not warming, not bacteria
items.ko_line: The receptor itself only responds to a molecule once it has changed state.
items.exp_title: A wet surface a dry molecule has to cross
items.exp_text: The receptor cells sit underneath a thin, constantly renewed film of mucus, and an odour molecule drifting through the air has to dissolve into that film before it can reach one. Dissolving is the step that lets the molecule fit into a receptor and trigger a signal, so a bone-dry nose smells nothing at all.

items.prompt: How can a nose tell apart thousands of different smells with a limited number of receptor types?

options.label: Each smell gets its own dedicated receptor
options.feedback: There are far more smells than there are receptor types, so a one-to-one match for every smell isn't possible.

options.label: One receptor type handles every smell, at different strengths
options.feedback: A single receptor type could only signal how strong a smell is, not what kind of smell it is.

options.label: Each molecule triggers its own particular combination of receptor types
options.feedback: A given molecule usually fits several receptor types at once, each to a different extent, forming a distinct pattern.

options.label: The nose only detects a handful of basic smells, mixed together
options.feedback: Unlike a short list of basic tastes, there's no small fixed set of 'basic smells' that everything else is built from.

items.ok_line: It isn't one receptor per smell — it's a pattern across many receptors at once.
items.ko_title: Not one-to-one, not a single dial
items.ko_line: With far fewer receptor types than there are smells, telling them apart has to come from a pattern, not a single match.
items.exp_title: A code built from combinations, not single keys
items.exp_text: Each receptor type responds, to some degree, to a range of molecular shapes rather than to just one, and a single odour molecule usually fits several receptor types at once, each to a different extent. The particular pattern of which receptors fire together, and how strongly each one responds, gives the nervous system a distinct combination to recognise for that molecule.

items.prompt: Why does taking a deliberate sniff help you smell something faint?

options.label: A sharp sniff pulls more air, and more odour molecules, up to the receptor patch
options.feedback: A sniff redirects the airflow, pushing a larger share of the breath up toward the receptors.

options.label: Sniffing warms the air before it reaches the nose
options.feedback: Warming the air doesn't change how much of it reaches the smell receptors.

options.label: Sniffing dries out the mucus so molecules pass through faster
options.feedback: Drying the mucus layer would make it harder for molecules to dissolve, not easier.

options.label: Sniffing increases the number of receptor cells working
options.feedback: The number of receptor cells stays the same from one breath to the next; sniffing changes how much air reaches them.

items.ok_line: A sniff changes where the air goes, not how many cells are waiting for it.
items.ko_title: Not temperature, not dryness, not more cells
items.ko_line: The receptors don't change — what changes with a sniff is the path the air takes.
items.exp_title: Short, sharp breaths that redirect the airflow
items.exp_text: Quiet, steady breathing carries most air along the floor of the nasal passage, well below the patch of smell receptors near the roof. A quick, sharp sniff changes that airflow pattern and pushes a larger share of each breath up toward the receptors, delivering more odour molecules to them than a normal breath would.

items.prompt: Why is the inside of your nose shaped with curled, bony scrolls rather than being one smooth open channel?

options.label: The scrolls trap dust like a filter net
options.feedback: Dust is caught mainly by hairs near the nostrils, not by the shape of these curled bones further inside.

options.label: The scrolls help the nose keep its shape from outside pressure
options.feedback: The outer shape of the nose is held up by cartilage nearer the surface; these bones sit deep inside.

options.label: The scrolls store extra air for holding your breath
options.feedback: No space in the nasal cavity is set aside for storing air; every breath simply passes through.

options.label: The scrolls stir the airflow so it swirls past more of the nasal lining
options.feedback: The curled shape breaks up a straight airflow, forcing it to swirl and brush across more of the lining.

items.ok_title: A swirl, not a straight shot
items.ok_line: A curled path forces air to brush past parts of the lining a straight tube would skip.
items.ko_title: Not dust, not structure, not storage
items.ko_line: Think about what shape does to the path the air actually takes.
items.exp_title: Curls that turn a straight draft into a swirl
items.exp_text: A smooth, straight channel would let air rush from nostril to throat along the shortest path, brushing past only a small part of the lining on the way. The curled, scroll-shaped bones break that straight line up, forcing the airflow to swirl and tumble as it passes through, so a larger share of each breath brushes across the lining — including the patch that detects smell.

items.prompt: Why does food taste so much blander when your nose is completely blocked?

options.label: A blocked nose changes how saliva breaks food down
options.feedback: Saliva keeps doing its job the same way whether the nose is blocked or clear.

options.label: Odour molecules from food can no longer reach the smell receptors through the back of the throat
options.feedback: A passage at the back of the throat normally lets odour molecules from chewed food drift up to the nose.

options.label: Blocking the nose numbs the tongue
options.feedback: The tongue's own sensors work independently of the nose and stay just as responsive.

options.label: A blocked nose lowers the temperature of food in the mouth
options.feedback: The temperature of food in the mouth comes from the food itself, not from airflow through the nose.

items.ok_line: Much of what registers as 'taste' is actually smell arriving from behind, through the throat.
items.ko_title: Not saliva, not numbness, not temperature
items.ko_line: Something that normally reaches the nose from inside the mouth is being cut off.
items.exp_title: A back-door route from mouth to nose
items.exp_text: Chewing releases odour molecules from food into the air inside the mouth, and there is a passage at the back of the throat that connects straight up into the nasal cavity, letting those molecules drift up to the smell receptors from behind. Block the nostrils and that back route closes along with the front one, so those molecules never make it up to the receptors, and flavour collapses down to what the tongue itself can sense.

items.prompt: Why does a strong smell in a room seem to fade the longer you stay in it, even though the source hasn't gotten weaker?

options.label: The odour molecules break down in the air over time
options.feedback: Most odour molecules stay chemically stable in the air for far longer than it takes for a smell to seem to fade.

options.label: The body produces a counter-smell to cancel it out
options.feedback: Nothing is released to neutralise or mask the odour; the change happens in the signal, not in the air.

options.label: The nose's receptors and the pathway carrying their signal reduce their response to an unchanging smell
options.feedback: A receptor exposed to a steady smell responds strongly at first and then gradually eases off.

options.label: Cold air numbs the receptors after a few minutes
options.feedback: The fading happens at any room temperature, equally in a warm room, so temperature isn't driving it.

items.ok_title: A response that quiets, not a smell that fades
items.ok_line: The molecules keep arriving; it's the signal reporting them that dims.
items.ko_line: If the smell were breaking down or being cancelled, a newcomer walking in wouldn't still smell it clearly.
items.exp_title: A signal that quiets when nothing changes
items.exp_text: A receptor exposed to a steady, unchanging smell responds strongly at first but then gradually eases off, the same way a repeated tap on the skin feels less noticeable than the first one. Because the response fades even though the molecules keep arriving at the same rate, a smell that was sharp on walking into a room can become almost unnoticeable after a while, even as a newcomer walking in fresh still smells it clearly.

items.prompt: What is unusual about the nerve cells that detect smell, compared with most other nerve cells in the body?

options.label: They are regularly replaced by new ones throughout life
options.feedback: Nearby cells keep dividing and maturing into fresh replacements, something most other nerve cells never do.

options.label: They never send any electrical signal at all
options.feedback: Sending an electrical signal onward is exactly their job — that part works the same as other nerve cells.

options.label: They can move around the body freely
options.feedback: They stay fixed in place within the nasal lining; what makes them unusual is how often they get replaced.

options.label: They are the only ones without any connection to a nerve fibre
options.feedback: Each one has its own long connecting fibre reaching further into the body; without it, its signal would go nowhere.

items.ok_line: Directly exposed to the outside air, these cells take damage most nerve cells never face — and get replaced because of it.
items.ko_title: They still fire, and they still stay put
items.ko_line: What's unusual isn't whether they signal or move — it's how long any one of them lasts.
items.exp_title: Cells directly exposed, and directly replaceable
items.exp_text: Sitting right at the surface of the nasal lining, these cells are directly exposed to whatever passes through the nose — dust, dry air, irritants — and take steady damage as a result. To make up for that wear, a supply of nearby cells keeps dividing and maturing into fresh replacements throughout a person's life, a trick that other nerve cells in the body are generally never able to pull off.

items.prompt: Why does warm food generally give off more smell than the same food cold?

options.label: Warmth makes the nose more sensitive
options.feedback: The receptors themselves work the same whether the room is warm or cool; the change happens at the food, not inside the nose.

options.label: Warm air carries sound and smell together
options.feedback: Sound and smell travel completely separately, and neither one changes how the other moves through the air.

options.label: Heat causes more of the food's molecules to escape into the air
options.feedback: Heating adds energy to the food's molecules, so more of them break free into the surrounding air.

options.label: Cold air destroys odour molecules on contact
options.feedback: Odour molecules aren't destroyed by cold; they simply stay put in the food rather than escaping.

items.ok_line: Heat doesn't create the smell — it just helps more of it escape into the air.
items.ko_line: The nose isn't what changes here; the food itself is releasing more of what it always had.
items.exp_text: Every substance constantly loses a few of its molecules into the surrounding air, and how many escape at once depends on how much energy those molecules have. Heating the food adds energy to its molecules, so more of them break free into the air around it and reach the nose, while a cold version of the same food releases them far more slowly.

items.prompt: Why can't you smell something that's sealed inside a closed jar?

options.label: The smell exists as a signal only, with no physical molecules involved
options.feedback: Every smell begins with actual physical molecules; there's nothing signal-like about it before they reach the nose.

options.label: Airborne molecules from the object can't reach your nose while the container stays shut
options.feedback: The seal simply traps the escaping molecules inside their own small pocket of air.

options.label: Glass blocks smell the way it blocks light
options.feedback: It isn't the material of the jar doing the blocking; a paper bag, sealed shut, would stop the smell just as completely.

options.label: The smell needs to be warmed by air outside the jar
options.feedback: Many strong-smelling things need no warming at all — the seal itself is what's keeping the smell in.

items.ok_line: It isn't the glass doing the blocking — it's the seal keeping the molecules from ever leaving.
items.ko_title: Not glass, not signals, not warmth
items.ko_line: A sealed paper bag would work just as well as a jar — so it isn't about the material.
items.exp_title: No molecules in the air, nothing to detect
items.exp_text: Smelling something depends on its molecules actually breaking free into the surrounding air and travelling to the nose, not on some property radiating outward independent of matter. A sealed jar simply keeps those escaping molecules trapped inside its own small pocket of air, so none of them ever reach the nose to be detected.
